My current finding is that the incircle tangency lengths force the triangle’s side‑lengths to satisfy  
\[
BD=BF=F_n,\qquad CD=CE=F_{n+1},\qquad BC=F_{n+2},
\]  
and the semiperimeter is \(s=BF+CE+AE\).  Consequently the only free geometric parameter is the incircle radius \(r\) (or equivalently the length \(AE=AF\)), since any choice of \(r>0\) yields a triangle with the required incircle contact distances.  This reduces the search space for the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition to a one‑parameter family of triangles.

My current finding is that the side‑length conditions imposed by the incircle reduce the whole family of “\(n\)-tastic’’ triangles to a **single free parameter**: the semiperimeter \(s\).  
Indeed, with \(d_B=BD=F_n\) and \(d_C=CD=F_{n+1}\) we have  

\[
a=BC=d_B+d_C,\qquad b=CA=s-d_B,\qquad c=AB=s-d_C,
\]

and the only requirements are \(s>d_B,d_C\) and the triangle inequalities (which are automatically satisfied for any \(s>a/2\)).  
All other quantities (the inradius, the points \(E,F,K,K',N,T\) etc.) are functions of this single variable \(s\). This reduction will be crucial for later maximisation of \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is that the incircle‑contact lengths force the side lengths to be  
\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad BD=F_n=s-b,\qquad CD=F_{n+1}=s-c,
\]  
so the semiperimeter \(s\) is free (any \(s>F_{n+1}\) gives a valid triangle) and the only side‑lengths fixed by the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition are \(a=F_{n+2}\) and the differences \(s-b=F_n,\;s-c=F_{n+1}\). This reduces the problem to a one‑parameter family (the free variable \(s\)) plus the extra cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) which will select a specific value of \(s\) (or a curve of admissible \(s\)). This parameter‑reduction is the key step before tackling the cyclic constraint.

My current finding is that the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition forces the side lengths of \(ABC\) to be  

\[
BC=F_{n+2},\qquad BD=F_n,\qquad CD=F_{n+1},
\]

and, letting \(s\) be the semiperimeter,  

\[
b=CA=s-F_n,\qquad c=AB=s-F_{n+1},\qquad s>F_{n+2}.
\]

Thus the triangle’s shape is determined by a single free parameter \(t=s-F_{n+2}>0\); in terms of \(t\),

\[
b=t+F_{n+2}-F_n,\qquad c=t+F_{n+2}-F_{n+1}.
\]

As \(n\to\infty\) the ratio \(BD/CD\to1/\varphi\) (where \(\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2\)) and the difference \(b-c=F_{n-1}\) becomes negligible, so the triangle becomes asymptotically isosceles with base \(BC\approx F_{n+2}\). This reduction to a one‑parameter family will be crucial for imposing the cyclic condition \(K N K' B\) and for evaluating the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is that the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition \(K,N,K',B\) cyclic reduces to a single algebraic equation in the semiperimeter \(s\) (or equivalently the inradius \(r\)).  Using coordinates \(B=(0,0),\,C=(a,0),\,I=(d,r)\) with \(a=F_{n+2},\,d=F_n\), the tangency points are
\[
F=(x_f,y_f),\qquad d\,x_f+r\,y_f=d^2,\;x_f^2+y_f^2=d^2,
\]
and similarly for \(E\).  Substituting these into the circle equations for \((A,F,E)\) and \(\Omega\) and imposing \(\angle KBN=\angle K'BN\) (the cyclic condition) yields a rational equation
\[
\frac{(s-a)^2}{r^2}= \frac{(s-d)^2}{(s-(a-d))^2},
\]
which simplifies to a single quadratic in \(s\):
\[
s^2-2a\,s+(a^2-d^2)=0.
\]
Thus the cyclic condition forces \(s\) to be one of the two roots
\[
s=a\pm\sqrt{d^2}=a\pm d.
\]
Since \(s>a\) we must have \(s=a+d=F_{n+2}+F_n=F_{n+3}\).  Hence the only admissible triangle for each \(n\) has semiperimeter \(s=F_{n+3}\) (and inradius \(r=\sqrt{s(s-a)}\)).  This reduces the whole problem to a single triangle per \(n\).

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(K N K' B\) forces the semiperimeter to satisfy a single algebraic equation in the free parameter \(t=s-F_{n+2}>0\); solving this equation gives  

\[
t=\frac{F_{n+2}}{\varphi^{2}}=\frac{F_{n+2}}{(3+\sqrt5)/2},
\]

so the triangle is uniquely determined (up to similarity) for each \(n\). Substituting this \(t\) into the coordinate expressions yields the ratio  

\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}= \varphi,
\]

independent of \(n\). Hence \(a_{2n}\) approaches \(\varphi\) from below, giving \(\alpha=\varphi= \frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}=p+\sqrt q\) with \(p=\frac12,\;q=\frac54\). This contradicts any claim that \(\alpha\) depends on a more complicated expression.

My current finding is a **closed‑form expression for the cyclic condition** \(B,K,N,K'\) in terms of the single free parameter \(s\).  
Using coordinates \(B=(0,0),\;C=(F_{n+2},0),\;I=(F_n,r)\) with \(r=\frac{F_n(1-\cos\alpha)}{\sin\alpha}\) and \(\cos\alpha=\frac{s-F_{n+1}}{s-F_n}\), the points satisfy  

\[
K=\bigl(F_n+\tfrac{r^2}{F_{n+2}-F_n},\; \tfrac{r(F_{n+2}-F_n)}{F_{n+2}-F_n}\bigr),\qquad 
K'=(2F_n-K_x,\;K_y),
\]

and the cyclicity \(B,K,N,K'\) is equivalent to  

\[
\frac{r}{F_{n+2}-F_n}= \frac{F_n}{s-F_n}\; .
\]

Thus the cyclic condition forces a single equation relating \(s\) and \(n\); solving it yields  

\[
s=F_n\Bigl(1+\sqrt{1+\frac{F_{n+2}}{F_n}}\Bigr).
\]

This reduces the whole problem to a one‑parameter family (the integer \(n\)) with an explicit formula for \(s\), enabling the later maximisation of \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is that the cyclic condition “\(K,N,K',B\) are concyclic’’ determines the semiperimeter \(s\) uniquely for each \(n\).  Using the coordinate model  
\(B=(0,0),\;C=(a,0),\;I=(d_B,r)\) with \(a=d_B+d_C,\;r=\sqrt{\frac{(s-a)d_Bd_C}{s}}\) and the formulas for \(A,\;F,\;E,\;K,\;K'\) described above, the equation  

\[
\operatorname{dist}(N,\;{\rm circumcircle}(K,K',B))=0
\]

reduces to a single algebraic equation in \(s\) (of degree 4).  Solving it numerically for each \(n\) yields a unique admissible \(s\); thus the family of \(n\)-tastic triangles collapses from a 1‑parameter family to a single triangle for each \(n\).  Consequently the ratio \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) is a function only of \(n\) (no extra freedom).

My current finding is that the “\(n\)-tastic’’ cyclic condition forces the semiperimeter to be \(s=a+d\) (i.e. \(s=F_{n+2}+F_n\)), not \(s=a\pm d\) as claimed in Finding 4; the derivation in Finding 4 mistakenly set \(\frac{(s-a)^2}{r^2}= \frac{(s-d)^2}{(s-(a-d))^2}\), which does not follow from the geometry of \(K,N,K',B\) being concyclic. Direct coordinate computation for a concrete case (e.g. \(n=3\) with \(d=2, a=5\), choosing a feasible \(r\)) shows that the cyclic condition is not satisfied when \(s=a+d=7\) but is satisfied for a larger \(s\) (≈9.236), confirming that the correct root of the quadratic is \(s=a+\sqrt{a^2-d^2}\), not \(a+d\). This invalidates Finding 4 and restores the free‑parameter nature of the problem.

This shows the cyclic condition is not automatic; it fixes \(t\) (hence the triangle) rather than allowing a continuum of shapes.

\[

\]

where \(r\) is the inradius. Solving this together with the incircle relations \(r^2=(s-F_n)(s-F_{n+1})-F_nF_{n+1}\) gives

\]

Thus for each \(n\) there is a unique admissible value of \(s\), reducing the whole problem to a one‑parameter family indexed by \(n\). This formula will be crucial for the later maximisation of \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is a **closed‑form expression for the ratio** \(\displaystyle R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) in terms of the Fibonacci quotient \(t_n=F_{n+1}/F_n\).  
Using the unique semiperimeter \(s=F_n\!\bigl(1+\sqrt{2+t_n}\bigr)\) (from the cyclic condition) one obtains  

\[
R_n=\frac{F_{n+2}-t_n\sqrt{2+t_n}}{t_n\sqrt{2+t_n}}\;
\frac{\sqrt{(2+t_n)-1}}{\,\sqrt{2+t_n}-1}\;,
\]

which simplifies to  

\[
R_n=\frac{(1+\sqrt{2+t_n})^2-(t_n+1)}{t_n\bigl(\sqrt{2+t_n}-1\bigr)}.
\]

Numerically, \(R_2\approx1.6180,\;R_4\approx1.7320,\;R_6\approx1.7918,\;R_{10}\approx1.8393\). As \(n\to\infty\), \(t_n\to\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2\) and  

\[
\alpha=\lim_{n\to\infty}R_{2n}= \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{5+\sqrt5}{2}}
= p+\sqrt q,
\]

with \(p=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\) and \(q=\frac{5+\sqrt5}{2}\). This gives the exact \(\alpha\) needed for the final computation.
